case_study_insert.main_stem: Redwood Gear Works (RGW) is a partnership in the precision engineering sector, employing a workforce of 35. Founded in 2005 by Callum Redwood and Imani Redwood, it makes custom gearboxes for renewable-energy converters and operates a hierarchical structure with laissez-faire leadership. RGW plans to invest $640,000 in a gear-grinding cell, financed by $240,000 partners' capital, a $250,000 bank loan and $150,000 of hire purchase. It has fixed costs of $210,000 a year, a variable cost of $9.00 a unit and a selling price of $16.00, and produces 60,000 units a year. RGW faces a rising scrap rate of 3.6% on gear blanks and a shortage of skilled grinders in its Bristol workshop.
case_study_insert.appendix_1_marketing_ops: Operations Log — Week 18 2025: The grinding cell completed 1,450 gear blanks with a scrap rate of 3.6%, compared with 2.1% in Week 10. Rework hours rose from 26 to 58 a week. Delivery promises were missed on 17 of 94 orders. A customer survey of 220 renewable-energy firms found 66% rate delivery reliability as critical and 39% had changed supplier after a missed order. A skills audit shows 7 of 35 workers are certified on the new grinding cell; a certification course costs $780 per person.

case_study_insert.appendix_3_external_environment: Economic and Business Bulletin (March 2026): (1) The central bank raised the base interest rate from 4.00% to 4.75%, raising costs on variable-rate borrowing. (2) The national minimum wage will rise by 6.4% from $12.60 to $13.41 per hour from April 2026. (3) Wholesale alloy-steel prices have risen 10.5% year-on-year, while engineering input inflation is 7.1% and orders from renewable-energy converters are forecast to grow 4.0%.

questions.question_text: RGW is financing its $640,000 grinding cell with $240,000 partners' capital, a $250,000 bank loan and $150,000 of hire purchase. Explain two advantages for RGW of using hire purchase rather than the bank loan for the equipment.
questions.model_answer:
Point 1: Hire purchase spreads the $150,000 cost of the grinding equipment into regular payments, so RGW keeps its $250,000 bank loan available as working capital. That matters when 17 of 94 delivery promises were missed and 39% of surveyed firms had changed supplier after a late order; the partnership needs cash to improve deliveries rather than tying it all up in machinery.

Point 2: With hire purchase RGW can use the asset immediately while paying for it, and the gear-grinding cell starts reducing the 3.6% scrap rate and 58 weekly rework hours right away. The $210,000 fixed-cost base is not increased by a second full loan, so the partners, Callum and Imani Redwood, retain more control and the $640,000 expansion can proceed even with only 7 of 35 workers certified. Hire purchase also matches payment to the life of the asset, so the partnership is not still paying for the cell once it is obsolete; with 17 of 94 orders late and 39% of surveyed firms having changed supplier, keeping the $250,000 loan free for delivery improvements is more valuable than extra equipment debt.

knowledge_max_2: 1 mark for each valid point identified (max 2).
application_analysis_max_6: Up to 3 marks per point for detailed contextual explanation and analysis applied to RGW.

questions.question_text: RGW is promoting its custom gearboxes. Consider a website catalogue with e-commerce, a trade journal advertisement, or a technical sales agent. Which should RGW choose to win renewable-energy orders? Justify your recommendation.
questions.model_answer:
Website catalogue with e-commerce: A site lets converters browse specifications, request quotes and place orders at any time, giving a small partnership of 35 a national reach without a sales team. It suits technical buyers who want data before speaking to anyone. The drawback is that the 66% of surveyed firms who rate delivery reliability critically cannot be reassured by a web page alone, and RGW currently misses 17 of 94 delivery promises, so a slick catalogue could attract orders it cannot fulfil.

Trade journal advertisement: An advert in a renewable-energy engineering magazine reaches the right technical readers and builds credibility cheaply. However, an advert is passive, cannot show custom tolerances in detail, and provides no mechanism for a buyer to check the 66% delivery concern. With $210,000 fixed costs and $150,000 of hire purchase payments, RGW cannot afford spend that generates enquiries rather than contracts.

Technical sales agent: An agent with engineering knowledge can visit converter manufacturers, discuss custom designs and confirm delivery schedules face to face. This directly answers the 66% who need reliability and the 39% who changed supplier after a missed order. The cost is commission and loss of direct control, and one agent can cover only a limited region.

Recommendation: RGW should choose a technical sales agent. Custom gearboxes need explanation and trust, and only an agent can address the delivery record that has already lost 39% of surveyed firms, while a website can be added later for repeat orders. The trade journal is rejected as too passive for bespoke engineering, and the website alone is rejected because it cannot overcome the 17 of 94 missed deliveries. RGW should pair the agent with a simple catalogue.

mark_scheme.level_1_1_to_4: Lists the three promotion methods with limited reference to RGW.
mark_scheme.level_2_5_to_8: Compares at least two methods using RGW's survey, delivery and cost data with some judgement.
mark_scheme.level_3_9_to_12: Evaluates all three methods in RGW's context, recommends the sales agent and explains why the website and journal are rejected.

questions.question_text: RGW's scrap rate is 3.6% and only 7 of 35 workers are certified on the grinding cell. Explain two benefits for RGW of laissez-faire leadership in this situation.
questions.model_answer:
Point 1: Laissez-faire leadership lets the seven certified grinders decide how to set up jobs without waiting for Callum or Imani Redwood, so the 1,450 gear blanks are processed with fewer delays. Their hands-on knowledge is closest to the 3.6% scrap rate, and fast local decisions can cut the 58 hours of weekly rework that a hierarchical manager might not notice quickly.

Point 2: Delegation gives skilled workers autonomy, which can motivate them and help RGW keep the scarce grinders it needs to expand the $640,000 cell. In a partnership with a workforce of 35, involving experts in scheduling also frees the partners to negotiate with renewable-energy converters, where 66% of buyers rate delivery reliability critical and 39% have already switched after late orders. Since 17 of 94 delivery promises were missed, delegating scheduling to the certified grinders lets them re-sequence urgent gearbox jobs immediately instead of waiting for a partner to approve each change.

knowledge_max_2: 1 mark for each valid point identified (max 2).
application_analysis_max_6: Up to 3 marks per point for detailed contextual explanation and analysis applied to RGW.

questions.question_text: RGW must close its grinding skills gap. Consider sending workers on the $780 external certification course or running an in-house mentoring programme led by the 7 certified operators. Which should RGW choose? Justify your decision.
questions.model_answer:
External certification course: At $780 per person, an externally certified worker gains a recognised qualification and up-to-date techniques, which reassures converters where 66% rate reliability critically. Certification is portable and proves competence. However, sending several of the 35 workers off-site reduces output of 1,450 gear blanks a week, worsening the 17 of 94 missed deliveries, and the full cost for the 7 of 35 not yet certified would be 28 × $780 = $21,840 — significant for a partnership with $210,000 fixed costs and $150,000 of hire purchase.

In-house mentoring: The seven certified grinders can train colleagues on the actual cell, so learning is specific to RGW's machines and no one leaves the Bristol workshop. It uses existing expertise, costs no course fee and allows training to fit around orders, helping to cut the 3.6% scrap rate and 58 rework hours without new spending. The drawback is that the quality of teaching depends on the mentors' communication skills, and there is no external certificate to show customers.

Decision: RGW should choose in-house mentoring first. It keeps all 35 workers on the job, avoids the $21,840 fee and attacks the 3.6% scrap rate on the exact equipment RGW uses; the external course is rejected for now because removing workers would deepen the 17 of 94 late deliveries. RGW can send the most able mentees for $780 certification later once reliability recovers. Because 17 of 94 orders were delivered late, keeping all workers in the workshop while they learn matters more than a certificate in the short term, and the 66% of buyers who rate reliability critically will judge RGW on deliveries, not paperwork.

mark_scheme.level_1_1_to_4: Describes the two training routes with little application to RGW.
mark_scheme.level_2_5_to_8: Analyses costs and benefits of one or both routes using RGW's scrap, delivery and workforce data.
mark_scheme.level_3_9_to_12: Evaluates both routes with explicit working, recommends in-house mentoring and clearly rejects the external course.

questions.question_text: Calculate and explain how RGW's management can use its cost, break-even and productivity data.
questions.model_answer: Formula: Break-even output = Fixed costs ÷ Contribution per unit. Substitution: $210,000 ÷ ($16.00 − $9.00) = $210,000 ÷ $7.00 = 30,000 units. | Formula: Contribution per unit = Selling price − Variable cost per unit. Substitution: $16.00 − $9.00 = $7.00. | (iii) Four contextual uses explained.

sub_parts.model_answer: Formula: Break-even output = Fixed costs ÷ Contribution per unit. Substitution: $210,000 ÷ ($16.00 − $9.00) = $210,000 ÷ $7.00 = 30,000 units. Answer: break-even output is 30,000 units a year.
Formula: Contribution per unit = Selling price − Variable cost per unit. Substitution: $16.00 − $9.00 = $7.00. Answer: contribution per unit is $7.00.

sub_parts.question_text: Explain four ways RGW's management can use this financial data.
sub_parts.model_answer:
1. Comparing break-even of 30,000 units with 60,000 produced gives a margin of safety of 30,000 units, so RGW can judge how much slack it has before expanding the $640,000 cell.
2. Contribution of $7.00 allows a discount decision: cutting $16.00 by $0.50 leaves $6.50, so $210,000 of fixed costs needs 32,308 units instead of 30,000.
3. Break-even of 30,000 units shows the volume needed before the $250,000 loan and $150,000 hire purchase can be serviced, guiding cash planning.
4. Unit cost of $210,000 ÷ 60,000 + $9.00 = $12.50 can be compared weekly with the 3.6% scrap rate and 58 rework hours to measure the cost of poor quality.

working_marks: 1 mark for the correct formula and 1 mark for the accurate numerical answer in (i) and (ii); 1 mark per valid applied use in (iii).

questions.question_text: Using Appendix 2, evaluate RGW's liquidity by calculating the current ratio and the acid test ratio for 2024 and 2025. Has RGW's liquidity improved? Justify your answer.
questions.model_answer:
Calculations:
Current Ratio 2024 = 1.46 : 1
Current Ratio 2025 = 1.97 : 1
Acid Test Ratio 2024 = 0.91 : 1
Acid Test Ratio 2025 = 1.22 : 1

Detailed workings: 2024 current assets = $95,000 inventories + $130,000 trade receivables + $30,000 cash = $255,000; 2025 current assets = $120,000 + $145,000 + $50,000 = $315,000. The broader liquidity measure is $255,000 ÷ $175,000 = 1.46 in 2024 and $315,000 ÷ $160,000 = 1.97 in 2025. Excluding inventories, the stricter measure is ($255,000 − $95,000) ÷ $175,000 = $160,000 ÷ $175,000 = 0.91 in 2024 and ($315,000 − $120,000) ÷ $160,000 = $195,000 ÷ $160,000 = 1.22 in 2025.

Evaluation: RGW's liquidity has improved substantially. Current liabilities fell from $175,000 to $160,000 while current assets rose by $60,000, lifting the broader measure from 1.46 to 1.97. More importantly, the stricter measure moved from 0.91 to 1.22, so the partnership can meet short-term obligations without depending on gear-blank inventories — vital while it services a $250,000 loan and $150,000 of hire purchase. The 2024 figure below 1.0 exposed a real cash squeeze. Still, inventories rose to $120,000 while the scrap rate is 3.6%, so some stock may be defective, and receivables of $145,000 are high relative to a business with $210,000 fixed costs and 17 of 94 late deliveries.

Conclusion: RGW's liquidity has improved. Both measures are higher and the stricter one now clears 1.0, showing a genuine strengthening rather than a stock-driven one. Management should monitor inventory quality and collect receivables promptly to protect the position.

mark_scheme.level_1_1_to_4: States isolated financial figures or vague comments about liquidity with no accurate ratio calculations.
mark_scheme.level_2_5_to_8: Calculates the current ratio and acid test ratio for both years with some contextual comment on the trend for RGW.
mark_scheme.level_3_9_to_12: Accurate ratio calculations for both years, detailed evaluation of inventories, receivables, cash and current liabilities, and a justified conclusion on whether RGW's liquidity improved.

questions.question_text: Explain one advantage and one disadvantage for RGW of recycling alloy-steel offcuts from its gear-grinding cell.
questions.model_answer:
Advantage: Collecting and selling swarf reduces waste and can offset part of the 10.5% rise in alloy-steel prices, protecting the $7.00 contribution per unit on 60,000 gearboxes. It also lowers disposal costs and supports the $640,000 grinding cell by making better use of materials, which matters when only 7 of 35 workers are certified and rework already runs at 58 hours a week.

Disadvantage: Separating alloy grades needs bins, storage and a buyer, adding work to a workforce of 35 that is already short of skilled grinders. Contaminated swarf fetches a low price, so savings may not cover the effort. With $210,000 fixed costs, $150,000 of hire purchase and a 3.6% scrap rate, RGW should first reduce scrap at source rather than spend partner time on recycling. The partners have already committed $240,000 of capital and $150,000 of hire purchase to the cell, so time spent sorting swarf has an opportunity cost in customer visits, especially when 66% of surveyed firms judge suppliers on delivery reliability.

knowledge_max_2: 1 mark for each valid point identified (max 2).
application_analysis_max_6: Up to 3 marks per point for detailed contextual explanation and analysis applied to RGW.

questions.question_text: Using Appendix 3, evaluate how the base interest rate rise to 4.75%, the 6.4% minimum wage increase and the 10.5% rise in alloy-steel prices will affect RGW. Which change will have the greatest impact? Justify your answer.
questions.model_answer:
Interest rate rise (4.00% to 4.75%): The rise is 0.75 percentage points. If the $250,000 bank loan is variable-rate, extra interest is 0.75% × $250,000 = $1,875 a year (0.0075 × $250,000); the $150,000 hire purchase may be at a fixed rate, so its cost need not change. Against $210,000 fixed costs this is modest, though it reduces funds available for the $640,000 cell.

Minimum wage increase (6.4%, from $12.60 to $13.41): Each hour rises by $13.41 − $12.60 = $0.81. RGW has a workforce of 35 but the insert gives no hours worked, so no annual total is defensible. Productivity is 60,000 units ÷ 35 = 1,714.29 units per worker; if that holds, the $16.00 price can absorb the rise. With only 7 of 35 certified and a 3.6% scrap rate, however, lower efficiency would raise unit cost quickly.

Alloy-steel inflation (10.5%): The $9.00 variable cost is not broken down in the insert, so an explicit upper bound is the honest approach: if all of it were steel-linked, 10.5% × $9.00 = $0.945, about $0.95 a unit; over 60,000 units that is roughly $56,700 a year. Even a fifth of that, about $11,340, is six times the loan interest increase and cuts directly into the $7.00 contribution while 58 weekly rework hours persist.

Conclusion: The 10.5% rise in alloy-steel prices will have the greatest impact. It affects every unit, cannot be neutralised by fixed-rate borrowing and erodes the contribution that funds both the loan and hire purchase. The interest rise is smaller and conditional; the wage rise is manageable if productivity stays near 1,714.29 units per worker.
